utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, please have the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: IT-94-A-1, the Prosecutor versus Tadic in the matter regarding allegations concerning prior counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The witness is being brought in. Mr. Registrar, subject to what counsel will advise, may I suggest that we save time if, in future cases, a part-heard witness and possibly even a fresh witness were seated before the Court assembles formally. No objection to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: No objection at all, Your Honour. In fact, I positively encourage it, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I will make sure this happens in the future, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, you are still under oath. You may be seated. Mr. Domazet, you were on your legs at the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, yesterday, towards the end of the day, we talked about the proceedings according to which a definite decision was passed, a definite ruling, with regard to Borka Vucic's charges brought against you. In those proceedings, it was concluded that you invented three interviews with her. You were heard in these proceedings, and the court did not believe you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: What is correct is that proceedings did take place before the district court in Belgrade at the request of Borka Vucic, and this was against the editor in chief of the newspaper Srpska Rec, and she wanted a denial to be published. This is the same court that is now in charge of the proceedings against the President of the United States, the Prime Minister of Great Britain, the President of France, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That was not my question.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I want this Court to understand what kind of a court we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Please, will you answer my questions?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is it true that the court ascertained that all three alleged interviews with Mrs. Vucic were false, invented, that she never actually talked to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: When the court establishes that a denial is supposed to be published, it does not state that something is right or wrong. It simply says that a denial has to be printed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, first the court established, and that is what it says in the elaboration of the verdict, that Mrs. Vucic never saw you, never talked to you, never gave you any one of these three alleged interviews with her?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: It is true that I was heard as a witness in those proceedings, and the other witnesses testified to the same thing. However, the question that the court was dealing with was whether legal requirements were met in terms of having her denial being published, and it is not for the court to ascertain whether information published is right or wrong; it is for the court to ascertain that a denial is supposed to be published. Any person is entitled to that. So no verdict was passed. There are proceedings that are taking place before the court of Judge Ana Popovic in the First Municipal Court in Belgrade. That is a fact too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, would you be so kind to answer counsel's question, which is this: Did the court make a finding that none of these three alleged interviews actually took place?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: The court did not pass such a ruling because they are not authorised to do so. According to the ruling that you have before you, the court decided the newspaper had to publish the denial of Mrs. Borka Vucic in respect of those texts. It is not for the court to decide whether the facts published in a text are true or false. That can be dealt with in criminal proceedings and in legal action taken before another court. In this particular court, the only decision that is supposed to be passed is whether, by law, it is necessary to publish a denial; that is to say, is there a person involved that has a justified interest in having a denial published in respect of a certain piece of news related to that particular person and whether this correction or whether this denial has something to do with that particular person in respect of that text. The court is not authorised to decide on anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It is precisely in this ruling, on page 5 -- may I please read that part of the ruling? It reads as follows: "The court established that the articles, 'I will die in a car,' 'Cobi is not owned by Milosevic' and also another article entitled 'Silk cord is waiting,' then also another article published in Srpska Rec, number 148, of the 22nd of April, 1996; 146, dated the 6th of May, 1996; and 150, dated the 20th of May, 1996, the court established that these articles are invented, that the party bringing charges," reference is made to Borka Vucic, "that she never gave any interview, nor did she conduct any conversation with Milovan Brkic, a journalist of this newspaper, that she never entered the premises of Srpska Rec, let alone engaged in a lengthy conversation with the director of this newspaper, Danica Draskovic, the editor in chief, Bogoljub Pejcic, and the journalist Milovan Brkic. The contents of these articles ..." et cetera, et cetera. The rest is not all that important.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Please, I would like to tender this into evidence. Yesterday, we tendered part of this ruling with an accompanying translation but not the entire ruling. However, because of the statement made by this witness, it is necessary to have a look at the entire ruling with the accompanying explanation and to present all of that as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Am I supposed to answer this? May I answer this?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It is not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me put this to you: Do you recognise that passage as part of the judgement in the case?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was not a party in these proceedings. I was one of the witnesses that was heard, in addition to the director of the newspaper, the editor in chief, and other witnesses. I was one of the witnesses. I made a statement there. Several persons corroborated that Mrs. Vucic came to the premises of Srpska Rec. We also gave a photograph that proved this. However, I have to repeat this: The court is only authorised to see whether there are conditions to publish the denial or the correction, and what the conclusion is, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The Tribunal has heard you on that point more than once. You have explained that you were only a witness and the case did not involve you as a party. Be that as it may, my question to you is this: Although you say you were only a witness, did you become aware of the judgement, and if so, did you recognise the passage read out to you by Mr. Domazet as part of the judgement?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, as a witness, I could not see the judgement. The judgement was received by the person who represented Srpska Rec, the lawyer of Srpska Rec. I'm surprised by this. According to the rules according to which courts operate, other persons are not entitled to get a judgement. I don't see how -- and you are going to be the judge of that -- this gentleman got a copy of the judgement. I, as a witness, was not entitled to a copy of the judgement. I don't know what the judgement says because I never read it in the original. I was only a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, the Bench wants to understand you. Should the Bench understand you to be saying this: that in your system, judgements are not publicly available documents?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. Absolutely. Only the parties involved can receive it; that is to say, the attorneys of those parties. I, as a witness, I could not receive a copy, and according to law, if the president of the Supreme Court issues a document stating that a particular party can have an interest in seeing the judgement or copying it, then that can be made possible. I don't see how come Mr. Vujin managed to produce some kind of document showing that he was entitled to see a copy of this judgement. Witnesses were heard in the proceedings between Srpska Rec and Mrs. Vucic. However, Mrs. Vucic has been dragging her feet on this because she did not want to be heard by the court, and we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, we've heard enough on that point. May I return the microphone to Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, quite a few of your articles are related to court proceedings, and you claim yourself that you are knowledgeable in these affairs, but we're going to prove this in another fashion. Judgments are accessible to all, especially this judgement, because it says explicitly that it's supposed to be published.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I do not know of this. However, the court has a copy of this judgement, so they will see for themselves. Nor was it ever publicly published.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: May I just say something? I've noticed whilst Mr. Brkic is being asked what are, frankly, lengthy questions containing assertions by my learned friend Mr. Domazet, whilst Mr. Brkic has been listening to those questions, he doesn't appear to have been provided with a copy of this judgement to be able to follow what's being read to him. I'm bound to say that is a concern of mine if this line of cross-examination is going to be pursued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We haven't got copies either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Neither have I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, do you have a copy in your hand?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. It is an exhibit read by Mr. Domazet, Exhibit 14, which is the same document as the document presented, numbered as Exhibit 12, but it is then the integral -- the total document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, is it possible for copies to be made available to the parties and to members of the bench?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is Exhibit number 14 and it is a document only in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, you have the document before you. Do you know the style of the judgement of your courts? Could you identify the document --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: -- and tell us whether you recognise it as a judgement of your courts?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, it is clear from this document that the court made it incumbent upon Mr. Bogoljub Pejcic to publish Vucic's denial and that's all. I haven't seen the rest; that is to say, the explanation provided by the court, the comments. That is up to the court. But what the ruling has to do with is simply this obligation of the editor in chief, Bogoljub Pejcic, to publish Mrs. Vucic's letter. That is the only thing they ruled on. The rest are comments and explanation. Probably the court is presenting its opinion. But it is not that they passed a verdict as to what the story carried in Srpska Rec is like or whether it's true or not. You're going to read that for yourself. It is only for Mrs. -- it was only made possible for Mrs. Vucic to have her denial printed. Mrs. Borka Vucic is a key figure of the Milosevic regime, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We have heard you, Mr. Brkic. Let's see where we have got to. You recognise that as a judgement of the court, leaving aside the issue how Mr. Domazet came by a copy of that document, may I ask you this: Do you see in that judgement the particular passage to which Mr. Domazet has been referring, a passage in which the court said that the alleged interviews never, in fact, took place?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that this has been highlighted. This is the comment of the court. On the contrary. Bogoljub Pejcic was not trusted and what he said was not believed, and Milan Brkic was not believed either. So that is how the court felt. However, I wish to say that this is the same district court that ruled that the president of the United States, of France, et cetera, were supposed to be held in custody right now. So that's the court we're talking about. So that court did not trust me. That's the only thing I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, you recognised the document as being in the style of a judgement of your courts. Are you questioning the authenticity of the document? Are you saying that the document is or is not really a judgement of the court?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: It is the judgement of the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. The Registrar is suggesting that the particular passage in the judgement be put on the ELMO and that perhaps it be read out by the translators.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be, if this is of assistance -- I thought Mr. Domazet was saying this morning that he was putting some extra papers before the court, but it may be that what's been asked about is what appears at page 618, 617, 616, and 615. I'm sorry to be counting backwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is it in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes. It may be that it is that he's referring to. With all due respect to Mr. Domazet, I'm not clear what article he's referring to. It may be that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me ask Mr. Domazet this question: Mr. Domazet, would it be possible for you to identify the particular portion of the judgement in which you're interested, and then we would have it put on the ELMO and I would ask the translators to read it out?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please read out the judgement in the B/C/S language from the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, would you read out the passage in B/C/S and then the translators will follow you and translate it in English and French? Mr. Brkic, would you look at the passage and satisfy yourself that Mr. Domazet is reading the passage before you?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, but I have one problem. I have no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You don't have --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I have only one copy of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: It's on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Could you read it from the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. [As read]: "In the statement of the plaintiff Borka Vucic" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: It's not coming through in English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I can hear you now. Yes, now it's perfect. Shall we start again?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. [As read]: "From the statement by the plaintiff Borka Vucic, who was heard as one of the parties in the case and whom the court completely believed, with a view to the fact that the same was logical and mutually linked up with the written documentations of the file itself in this legal case, and quite certainly she was convincing in this particular matter so that the court had no reason not to trust her. "The court ascertained that the articles entitled 'I Will Die in a Car', or 'Cobi is Not Milosevic's Property', or 'The Silk Noose is Waiting,' published in the newspaper Srpska Rec, number 148, dated the 22nd of April, 1996; number 149, dated the 6th of May, 1996; and number 150, of the 20th of May, 1996, were invented articles that the plaintiff never gave any interview whatsoever, nor did she have any kind of conversation with the journalist writing for the paper, Milovan Brkic, that she never set foot in the editorial offices of the newspaper Srpska Rec, let alone that she spent some lengthy time there in a discussion with the director of the editorial board of this newspaper, Danica Draskovic, and the accused and editor in chief Bogoljub Pejcic, and journalist Milovan Brkic, and that the contents of these articles are profoundly insulting to her honour and position and esteem, both in the country itself and abroad, undermining what she has achieved through many years of work and through her life. "By listening to the plaintiff as a party in the court case, the court has ascertained that from his fax machine in Nicosia -- from her fax machine in Nicosia, she sent three corrections, which have been appended to the case and are to be located in the files of this court case, and that the accused, not a single text -- published a single text of these three connections and amendments given. "On the contrary, the court did not believe the statement made by the accused Bogoljub Pejcic, who was heard as a party in the case, and witness Milovan Brkic, as they were illogical and mutually contradictory, and even if they were put forward by the accused and testified to the same circumstances and facts, and when they made their statements they were insecure in presenting them. They were not convincing and left the impression that they were hiding the truth." "In answer to the accusations, and the power of attorney has remained as it was, the accused will make corrections of the information received and given by the plaintiff as the plaintiff wrote them down, but she is required to send them to the accused once again so as this can be fully complied with." If it please Your Honour, you have this on page 616 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Part of it, about the last six lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Whilst I'm on my feet, if I may express my concern. What appears to have been read out is an extract which has never been translated in the documents submitted to this Chamber, only, as I say, the last six or seven lines under the heading, in the English translation I have at 616, "Explanation," and that in itself is part of a document purporting to be a decision of the District Court in Belgrade. The part headed "Judgement," and I'm looking at page 618, the part headed "Judgement," if I may just read it: "The request by the prosecutor Borka Vucic is accepted, and the accused Bogoljub Pejcic, as editor in chief of the newspaper 'Srpska Rec', is bound to publish in the first or second following issue of the magazine, after receiving the written Judgement, in the same manner as the texts that were published in ... 'I will die in the car' ... 'Silk cord is waiting,' the following correction:" There is then large chunks in inverted commas which say this, for example: "Regarding the article in the articles identified titled 'I will die in the car', written by Milovan Brkic, pursuant to the provisions of Article 31 of the Law of the Public Information, I submit my denial. Pursuant to the mentioned Law, I oblige you to publish the denial in the following issue of 'Srpska Rec'" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Abell, you are making a long statement. Are you objecting to something that Mr. Domazet is doing?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm simply concerned that what the Court has had read out under "Explanation" is one thing, but what the court apparently ordered -- I'm sorry to have taken time over it, but I needed to just explain -- what the court apparently ordered was that a denial by the person spoken of in the article should be published. That's what the court appears -- if I've understood it correctly from the partial translation I've received of it, that's what the court apparently ruled, merely that the newspaper should publish a denial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The bench would give you a chance to sum up in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: At this point, the bench, I think, is only interested in the reasoning of the court which led to that order for publication of a denial.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I quite understand that. I simply wanted to make sure that the Court knew the nature of the document or parts of which are being referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, do you recognise this document sent to the First District Court in Belgrade by the editor in chief of the newspaper Vecernje Novasti, a lawyer, Toma Fila, and the other journalists listed here?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I would like to have this document shown to the witness. It is in Serbian and it has an English translation.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: If you read the judgement out to me, could I now present my own views, if I may?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: With regard to the former judgement, we did not ask for your opinion.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Then I don't know why you read the judgement out to me. You should have just read it out to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We've passed that stage now. Was there something you wanted to say on the judgement which Mr. Domazet read out? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I would like to say that the judgement was brought by a judge who is a member of the main board of the ruling party, the Socialist Party, and that many people were heard before this court who have confirmed that Mrs. Vucic gave the interview and that Mrs. Vucic denied this, but that all our statements and testimonies were assessed as unconvincing, as can be seen, and that is the assessment of a court. I don't know how -- I don't think I need comment on that kind of judgement, with all due respect to the court in Belgrade as it stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Can you now recall the last question posed by Mr. Domazet and answer it, or shall I invite Mr. Domazet to repeat his question? Mr. Domazet, would you kindly repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In the Court of First Instance in Belgrade, is there proceedings against the editor in chief of Vecernje Novasti, Mr. Toma Fila, Attorney at Law, and other individuals with regard to the charges that I am having shown to you? Do you know about the action taken and has it been concluded?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will be marked Exhibit 15.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about this because I am not a party in the case. It is true that I am the author of the text that has been incriminated, but had there been a judgement and ruling, I would have been invited to be a witness and testify as author of the text. But I do recognise the stamp and seal of the court itself, and this charge was brought in 1995 by the following plaintiffs. Had a judgement and ruling been made, I would have quite certainly been called as a witness to testify because a judgement could not have been made without my own testimony, as I was the author of the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is that an admitted exhibit before the Court? Is that an exhibit before the Court?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it has just been marked, and it has, I think, the number 606 in the other document.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: If I may, I have just remembered something. It is true that Lawyer Rajko Danilovic, who is the lawyer for Srpska Rec, did show me a judgement whereby the First Municipal Court in Belgrade rejected the charge because Attorney Fila did not know how to write the document in proper legal manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, do you still write for the newspaper, Srpska Rec, today?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: How long did you go on writing for the newspaper?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I stopped a year ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell us the reasons why you ceased to work for Srpska Rec?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, because I work for other newspapers now, and that is the main reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What newspaper do you work for now, if you can tell us that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I am going to show the court my journalist ID card and I think that all the relevant data is in it. I work for a foreign employer, so I would prefer not to answer that question, but I will show you my ID. I am a member of the International Journalists' Association, and I'm sure you can check this out through the proper channels.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, I apologise for asking you that. I just wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I'm working for a foreign paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When did you publish your last article in Yugoslavia, in a Yugoslav newspaper? What was that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, I give interviews frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Not interviews; I mean articles written by you.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, I think the last time was three or four months ago. It is war now, and a law was passed on public information, and that is that in 24 hours all your property can be confiscated. So it can be seized within 24 hours. So this is a difficult situation, and I would bring into question my life, the property of editors, and some of them lost their lives in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So is that the reason why you no longer write?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: The reason I no longer write is the law on public information in Serbia in which every citizen can bring charges against you before a magistrate, which has 24 hours to bring in a decision and ruling. If the court concludes that you are in error, and they can do this, they can have a sitting at midnight or 1.00 a.m., then you are fined $100.000 or 200.000 marks, you go to prison straightaway. You do not have the right to complain. It is usually just one magistrate, just when you -- the procedure is the same if you're crossing the road drunk. That's the same thing. I think the international public is well aware of the restrictive rule of that kind that is in force in my country governing public information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, you said that you did write an article three or four months ago. Did you have any unpleasantness in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: No, I did not have any unpleasantness because the censor on duty was not fully alert, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you tell us what article, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: The article was in the newspaper called Blitz.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: During your career as a journalist did you write for Balkan Express?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was the editor in chief of that newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yesterday, when you talked about Mrs. Borka Vucic, you said that she was on the list of persons that cannot travel abroad, according to a list published by the European Union. Did you personally see this list?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it. It was published in our newspapers quite a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The entire list?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, the entire list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If you saw this list, did you see on that list the name of Bogoljub Pejcic, the editor in chief of Srpska Rec of whom you spoke with high regard yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know why he is on that list if this is, as you said, an opposition newspaper, a newspaper that is in opposition to the regime?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejcic received information from a commission that he addressed, and since he is an MP in the Serbian parliament, and during one month he was chairman of the committee for security and he was replaced very quickly, after a month only, and that is the explanation I was given. That is why Mr. Pejcic was put on this list. But if he is guilty and the international community has proof that he did something wrong, there is no reason why he shouldn't be held accountable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, in the Tadic case, you said that you had quite a bit of information as to who the investigator was and who statements were given to. Do you know the time during -- when Mr. Vujin took over this case?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, as soon as the Yugoslav authorities decided to extradite Mr. Tadic, a tournament was organised and Mr. Tadic was taken away, and the people who took him there handed him over to the German police so that they would see what the proceedings in The Hague Tribunal would be like and how they could affect them and what they could do about it, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, now that you mention this, I wanted to ask you about it anyway. Yesterday you said that it was the Serb police that handed over Tadic to the German police.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic knows who took him to this karate tournament.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, the people here probably know that, but I'm asking you how you received this information. Is it the same source that you spoke of yesterday or a different source?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, I'm going back to the question you put yesterday. You did not give a definite answer. That is to say, from the moment of Mr. Tadic's arrest in Germany, if I understood you correctly, do you know until when Mr. Vujin was his defence attorney?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot give you a specific answer, because I did not really ask for such details from the source I talked to and I was not really all that interested. And of course, this man would not have been pleased had I been putting all these extra questions, because he would say, "I'm telling you all this important stuff and now you're asking about this."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, it's the state security, you said.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, I personally am not that interested in all the details. If I was all that interested I could have read about it in the newspapers, but I'm personally not interested in such facts. So I'm not interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Vujin defended him at all in the initial proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, what I know is that Mr. Vujin was -- I don't know whether he was formally engaged, but I know that from the very outset, from Mr. Tadic's arrest, he was involved in the case, either through contacts with his family or in another way, but it was his obligation to be actively involved in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know that there were interruptions in his participation in this case?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Privately I heard that Mr. Tadic was unsatisfied with Mr. Vujin's defence and that he took the power of attorney away from him. In Belgrade, rumour had it that he bought Mrs. Tadic an apartment from the money that he got from the Tribunal, and these are vast amounts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know exactly how much money he got from The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, but I'm sure that the court has its own records.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you publish this amount in any of your articles?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it's about a couple of hundred thousand German Marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: My question was whether you published this in any one of your articles.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I mentioned it in any one of my articles, but I think I mentioned it in some of my interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In the evidence here we have your article from the beginning of 1995, your article concerning The Hague Tribunal. Did you write any other articles about the work of this Tribunal in The Hague, and if you did, when and where?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I'm a journalist who is involved in engaged journalism. I write an article or two every week. To tell you the truth, I do not recall. It's the same if you asked a driver whether five years ago he drove on the main street or a small street and which traffic-light he reached. I don't know. I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Before you came to The Hague yesterday, or one of these days when you came here, were you ever in The Hague before?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I was, at the invitation of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And you were in the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell us when this was?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I was in the Tribunal at the time when the proceedings were initiated against Mr. Vujin.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When Mr. Vujin was here?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: No. Mr. Vujin informed the court that he was busy and that he couldn't show up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you need this for your police report?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Don't worry, our police knows about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Please. I have nothing to do with the police.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: So why are you interested in my stay at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Maybe it's important for us. You said that you made a statement to Mr. Bozovic, an attorney. Did you make this statement here in The Hague or in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: In Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yesterday, in your statement, you mentioned that you knew that Mr. Vujin wrote written reports to the state security about his work in The Hague. What proof do you have of such allegations?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: This was given to me by this man who read these reports and who decided which of the state leaders he should send them to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is this the same source that you already referred to?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In your statements, and in your written statement to Mr. Bozovic, and Exhibit 10 that is mentioned here, you said not only from Mr. Vujin but also from Mr. Fila and Mr. Guberina, you said that -- I'm quoting you, I'm quoting the translation I got: "They are old informers of the secret police."

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I were in Serbia and if I were asked about this, to prove this would be as if you were trying to prove that water was wet. Everybody knows this. Only in Belgrade we have at least 2.500 lawyers. In this text that I wrote five years ago, I said who would be coming to the Tribunal, and this proved to be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You probably know that precisely Mr. Guberina, Mr. Fila, and Mr. Vujin are the three last presidents of the bar association of Serbia. That is to say, Mr. Guberina, Mr. Fila, and Mr. Vujin, exactly in that order. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, that just shows what the situation is like in Serbia. You cannot be a receptionist in a hotel unless your credentials have been checked out. Being president of the bar, that means that you are highly trusted by the regime and that you're in constant contact with the regime; otherwise it wouldn't have been possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know that the president of the bar association is elected by the lawyers themselves and exclusively by secret ballot and that this is done in a procedure involving several candidates and that is how all the three above-mentioned persons were elected?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Vujin has been holding this office for the past few years and that elections were never held, because the lawyers wrote a petition concerning this. They said that their assembly could not be convened. Only a hundred persons would come rather than 2.500, and they could not have a proper assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So your claim is that Mr. Vujin was not elected in this way by secret ballot?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Of course he wasn't. You know that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, I'm not a witness here, so it's not for me to say, but, yes, I do know.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, you're asking me and I'm answering as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know who the vice-president of the bar association of Serbia is now, either during this term or the last term?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: No. I wasn't really interested in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I am this vice-president and that's why I know.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Oh. Oh. Thank you for telling me. Wow. You should just bring in Igor Pantelic and that will round off things nicely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, I hardly know this man, and I'm not a lawyer in Belgrade, but I've been a lawyer for 30 years, and if you want to know the facts, I am in opposition to the regime, but I'm not sure about you, but we're not going to go into all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I apologise to the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I put a question related to the evidence, that is to say, that these three highly distinguished lawyers are, according to you, informers of the secret police. If I understood you correctly, you say this is a well-known fact but you have no other proof of this.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I think I published about 30 articles about Mr. Guberina, and I started this series sometime in 1989. Whether he sold off his clients, and whether he delivered them, and -- he never denied this. At some press conference he said that he could not bring charges against me because I'm not a citizen, because I don't have a registered place of residence anywhere. So it's probably the police that told him that my residence was not in Belgrade. And that's what he was asked, and he said, "He's not a citizen and he has no address."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, the court has listened to this last question and is wondering whether your cause might be better served by focusing on matters of greater relevance to the issue, and that is as to the knowledge which the witness has of Mr. Vujin's conduct in relation to this case. Would you, at the same time, like to indicate to us how much longer you will be? This question I ask only from the point of view of the managerial functions which the court must discharge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We're not in any way hurrying you up or urging you to curtail your --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour, but I'm really at the end of my --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I appreciate the suggestion made to me by the Honourable President of the Chamber, and I want to ask you whether you know more than you said about the Tadic case, that is to say, the role of Mr. Vujin and his work in this case, or whether everything you told us so far is everything you actually know about this.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I answered all the questions that were put to me and in this way I gave answers to these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Brkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, I would just ask you one or two questions. You spoke of a number of cases which were brought against you or in connection with your work. I think 570 cases. Some were dismissed on the basis of an argument that they were time barred or statutorily prescribed or on other technical grounds. Were any of these cases dismissed on the merits?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I think that I have understood your question. About 570 cases, criminal cases and civil cases. I hope that the distinction is clear between civil and criminal in the Yugoslav context. As far as I know, only five are still ongoing. All the others have been settled and I have been acquitted. I lost only one case, that is to say, not me but Srpska Rec, following a charge by Mr. Marko Milosevic, the son of the president of the Republic, and we were fined 140.000 dinars, which is the equivalent of approximately 10.000 German Marks. All the other cases -- I was acquitted in all the other cases, and five or six were dismissed for formal reasons, official reasons such as -- of Mr. Fila's charges, because he was not capable of writing them in the proper legal manner. So the court rejected them, and the court made it incumbent upon the plaintiffs to write the charges as befits charges in a court of law. The others are still pending, still ongoing, and I cannot tell you that in advance, but in all the other cases the court determined the facts and found that there were no grounds for pronouncing me guilty. Sometimes I was found guilty of impinging upon the dignity of individuals who brought charges against me. As far as the charges brought by Mr. Vujin and the other lawyers in the text, they seek for remuneration. They seek 10.000 dinars, which is about 800 German Marks, for their dignity and infringement upon their dignity. And that is the price of their dignity, I take it: 800 German Marks. Just to show you how far they assess their own dignity, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, tell the court a little about the case in which the Yugoslav District Court held that a certain story had been invented. Did the newspaper appeal from that decision?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know the fate of that appeal, but for you to understand the judgement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That answers my little question. You don't know whether there was an appeal. My question was whether there was. Now, the other thing --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Please. I do apologise. For Srpska Rec this was not an important case, because the court made it incumbent upon Srpska Rec just to publish Mrs. Vucic's letter. Usually it would publish reactions by the individuals, but as Mrs. Vucic sent her fax -- her letter by fax, it was not signed by her, so for these reasons her corrections were not published. But of course it was in our interests and the readers' interests to publish all corrections, denials and so on, but the Judges used this to comment, and by law the Judges were not authorised to do so because this was meritoriously done by a judgement, or ruling, or fine enforced, but in this kind of case the court took it upon itself to comment on our testimony, something which it is not entitled to do by Yugoslav law. So that is just what I wanted to say by way of clarification, because this was a precedent by the court in commenting on testimony and statements made by the witness, which were not essential in bringing about a ruling, in fact, and contrary to legal practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you for giving me the reasons why you consider there was no appeal. Now, tell the court a little about the extent of the circulation of Srpska Rec in which your article appeared, your article of the 13th March, 1995. Was this a daily newspaper or a weekly journal?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: It is a magazine and is a bimonthly. It comes out twice a month. I don't know the exact circulation. Twice a month, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Was the circulation of a kind which would suggest to you that Mr. Vujin was likely to see that particular issue?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't like saying this, but in the state in which I live, to publish any kind of fact bringing into question the integrity of the key figures of the regime is tantamount to pronouncing one's own death sentence. The Srpska Rec was one of the rare newspapers willing to publish other people's views. Most of the newspapers, TV stations, are under the most direct control of the Milosevic regime. They have a monopoly over the imported paper. They control the printing presses, which are state-owned. If you want to put out a paper, to print a paper, you have to buy paper from the regime. You have to go to their distribution network, because they -- and sell in their kiosks. So this is all absolutely under the control of the regime. So Srpska Rec is printed in a private printing press, in Glas, in Vlajkoviceva Street. It is a modest printing house, of modest capacity, and the Srpska Rec newspaper is read and photocopied. So that when it comes out in a photocopy -- it had more photocopies, in fact, than copies in circulation. So the circulation was much bigger than the actual copies put out. So for every one copy you would have at least ten photocopies. My articles in the Srpska Rec were the most largely quoted articles in foreign newspapers, and over the past twelve years I gave about 170 interviews to world newspapers, such as The New York Times, The Washington Post, Le Monde, and all the leading --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, I'm talking not about your interviews but about that particular publication. You have said that it was possible for photocopies to be made in the ratio of 10 to 1. Can you tell the Court this: What was the geographical base of the publication? Was the newspaper published in Belgrade? How many copies were published initially?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: It is published in Belgrade. I think the circulation is small compared to Dutch circumstances, 20.000. The circulation was 20.000. Those are the capacities of the printing press and printing house. Other magazines in Serbia are published in the circulation of between 10.000, 15.000. Due to the economic crisis and consumers -- powers of purchase, it goes up to 25.000. Circulation is 25.000 at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Anything on that? Thank you very much. Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I might, we still find ourselves a bit confused about the time frame in which the particular discussions with his source may have taken place. We would like, if the Court permit, two or three very brief and direct questions to clarify this time frame because we have a specific time frame as well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What you're saying to the Court is that this aspect was not before you at the time when you examined the witness; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: We attempted to elicit the information, Your Honour, and we don't believe we were very successful. We find ourselves still confused about this aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: But you did have an opportunity to examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You want a second opportunity?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Just very briefly on the time frame issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would that require the Court to give a similar opportunity to Mr. Domazet and Mr. Abell, do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I would imagine it would be up to them whether they found anything new in the questions which we asked, but we intend to focus strictly on the time frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I'm only sitting in the middle. Let me confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, my colleagues are with you, subject to your colleagues on the other side being afforded an opportunity to reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Further questions by Mr. Keegan:

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, I wanted to focus just specifically on the time frame in which your discussions with your source from the SDB took place, the discussions you referred to yesterday. First, let me ask you: When is it that you spoke with your source from the SDB about Mr. Vujin's alleged activities in Prijedor? Can you remember the time frame, the approximate date?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I think that in answering questions before this Tribunal, I have already said that my first talks were before the publication of the text in Srpska Rec, and the text was published in March 1995, that is to say, one to one and a half months prior to that, I had talks with the source about the planned activities of the service in engaging attorneys. I talked to him on several occasions later on, which I couldn't specify now, as to the activities of the lawyers in The Hague. So I can't tell you of those subsequent talks now. I didn't attach importance to those events and that I would have to bear this out before anybody. So I can't tell you the exact time of that. It escapes me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I may now, I want to be very clear with you. The discussions involving Mr. Vujin and what he may or may not have done in Prijedor with respect to interviewing witnesses, when were those discussions held, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I talked to the man from the State Security Service on several occasions. I had several contacts, not only with respect to the participation of the lawyers themselves, but I would frequently receive information which I then made public. I can't remember now what information and what facts I received during which particular talk, whether it happened in August or April. I can't orientate myself in time that precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. What year are we speaking of? Can you recall that? Were all your discussions within the same year?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: No, no. I had at least 20 talks every year, at least 20 talks per year with that particular source. Now, in which year, month, day in this case I devoted attention, I really can't tell you exactly. I know that it was not this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you make contemporaneous notes of your conversations with this source?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you have retained those notes?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: I could take a look. I keep my notes at my friend's places because it is quite normal in our country for our homes to be ransacked and searched.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just to clarify a point you made earlier when being questioned by Mr. Domazet, this source that we're speaking of, the one who informed you of Mr. Vujin's activities in Prijedor, this is the same source who told you that Dusko Tadic was extradited or turned over by Yugoslav authorities to the German authorities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that our authorities wanted to start having contacts with the Tribunal, and so they selected Mr. Tadic and took him to a competition of some kind and then told somebody to recognise him, a man who was a professional policeman in our police force, a member of the Associated Leftist Party of Yugoslavia, the YUL Party of Merdana Markovic. So they needed somebody who would do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Abell?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Could I just please clarify one matter as a result of what my learned friend has said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Just one matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I will be very brief, I hope. I'm grateful. Further questions by Mr. Abell:

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, you were just asked some questions to see if you could pin down the date when you had conversations with your source about Mr. Vujin, and I think you said you would have had maybe 20 meetings of that sort of order. You told me --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Per year.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Per year. Thank you. You told me, during the course of my questions of you yesterday, that amongst the topics you discussed was Mr. Vujin's involvement in the Tadic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Abell, how is this relevant to the question of the time frame?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Because I'm going to ask him right now if he can say when that was. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would some of those conversations have been last year, in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you remember --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Please, I can't quite know what conversation took place at what time, in which period, what I talked to my source about, what particular subject matter, because, as I say, I had contacts with him, and that is my job, to be able to obtain information, because the sources of information are closed in Yugoslavia, and you can't come by information in any other way, unless you have some personal contacts and sources who are, of course, high-risk ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All I'm seeking to clarify is this: Is it your evidence that in 1998, you would have had conversations with your source in the secret service concerning what Mr. Vujin was up to in the Tadic case?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BRKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin. The translation came in as "Vujic." It's Vujin. The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then that ends the case so far as this witness is concerned. The witness may now stand down, I believe. Nobody needs the witness any further. The witness may stand down. He's excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The sitting is suspended for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: at 5.45 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 2nd day of September, 1999, at 10 a.m.
